value.overview: The Northern Emerald-Toucanet is a medium-sized, vividly green member of the toucan family. It has a large bill whose black, yellow, white, and sometimes reddish pattern varies geographically, plus rusty tips to the tail feathers. Usually found in humid forest, it moves through the canopy and understory in pairs or small groups. It is an important fruit-eater and seed disperser, but also takes insects and small vertebrates.
value.classification: The Northern Emerald-Toucanet belongs to the toucan family, Ramphastidae, in the order Piciformes. Its scientific name is Aulacorhynchus prasinus. Some taxonomic treatments recognize blue-throated birds from Costa Rica and western Panama as a separate species, the Blue-throated Toucanet, Aulacorhynchus caeruleogularis; the name used here follows the selected classification.
value.identification: This toucanet is about 30–33 cm long and mostly grass-green, with a comparatively short tail and a large, laterally flattened bill. The bill typically shows black and yellow, with regional variation in the amount and placement of pale or reddish color. Rusty tail tips are often visible from below. In Costa Rica, blue-throated forms may show a noticeable blue patch on the throat. It is generally unmistakable where it occurs, although lighting can make its green plumage appear darker or bluer.
value.rangeHabitat: The species complex ranges from southern Mexico through Central America to Panama and nearby northern Colombia. In Costa Rica, Northern Emerald-Toucanets occur mainly in humid mountain forests, cloud forest, foothill forest, and wooded edges, especially in the central and southern highlands; they are also recorded in mature secondary forest, shade coffee, plantations, and other landscapes retaining substantial tree cover. They may occur from relatively low elevations locally to about 3,000 m, but are most characteristic of foothills and highlands.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally nonmigratory in Costa Rica and remains present year-round. Individuals may make local or seasonal movements along mountain slopes, shifting between elevations as weather, fruit availability, and breeding conditions change.
value.breeding: Breeding records in Costa Rica extend mainly from March through August, although timing can vary with elevation and local conditions. The species nests in a tree cavity, often a natural hole or an abandoned woodpecker cavity, and may enlarge the entrance. The female usually lays three or four eggs. Both parents incubate the eggs and feed the young, with incubation lasting about 16 days and the nestling period approximately six weeks.
value.dietFeeding: Fruit forms the largest part of the diet, including fruit from many tropical tree species. The bird usually forages from a perch in the canopy or upper understory and may swallow fruit whole, later regurgitating or passing the seeds. It also eats insects, centipedes, and other invertebrates, as well as small lizards, snakes, bird eggs, and nestlings. Animal prey is especially important when feeding growing young.
value.behavior: Northern Emerald-Toucanets are active, agile forest birds that commonly travel and forage in pairs or small groups, sometimes joining groups of several individuals. They move through foliage by short flights and deliberate hops, searching branches and fruiting trees. Their calls include repetitive, harsh, barking or yelping notes and lower, growling sounds. Pairs may exchange food, and both adults participate in nest care. The species also helps regenerate forests by dispersing seeds.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is believed to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.
